content: Urinary schistosomiasis is caused by an intravascular infection with the parasitic worm Schistosoma haematobium. The adult worms migrate to the venous plexus of the human bladder, where they release eggs. These eggs are excreted in the urine of the infected individual. Chronic infection can lead to significant morbidity and long-term complications, as the eggs become trapped in human tissues, causing inflammation and fibrosis. The efficacy and safety of drugs for treating urinary schistosomiasis were evaluated. The primary outcomes assessed were parasitological failure, defined as the continued presence of S. haematobium eggs in the urine more than one month after treatment, and the percentage reduction in egg counts from baseline. Data from randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were analyzed, and the quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE approach. A total of 30 RCTs involving 8,165 participants were included in the review. Most of these trials were conducted in children in sub-Saharan Africa, and many were over 20 years old. The quality of the studies was often unclear due to insufficient descriptions of study methods. Praziquantel: A single 40 mg/kg dose of praziquantel reduced the proportion of individuals excreting eggs in their urine by approximately 60% compared to placebo at one to two months post-treatment (Risk Ratio [RR] 0.42, 95% Confidence Interval [CI] 0.29 to 0.59; 864 participants, seven trials; high-quality evidence). The cure rate with praziquantel varied between trials, ranging from 22.5% to 83.3%, but in five of the seven trials, it exceeded 60%. Additionally, the mean number of schistosome eggs in the urine was reduced by over 95% in five out of six trials (678 participants, six trials; high-quality evidence). Splitting the 40 mg/kg dose into two doses over 12 hours did not provide additional benefits compared to a single dose. However, the split dose was associated with more adverse effects, such as vomiting (RR 0.5, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.86) and dizziness (RR 0.39, 95% CI 0.16 to 0.94), in a single trial involving 220 participants. Metrifonate: A single 10 mg/kg dose of metrifonate reduced egg excretion at eight months (210 participants, one trial). However, it was only slightly more effective than placebo in achieving cure at one month (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.74 to 0.94; 142 participants, one trial). In a trial comparing one, two, and three doses of metrifonate, the cure rate improved from 47% after one dose to 81% after three doses (93 participants, one trial; low-quality evidence). Two small trials compared a single 40 mg/kg dose of praziquantel with two or three doses of 10 mg/kg metrifonate. No clear differences in cure rates were observed (metrifonate 2 x 10 mg/kg at one month: RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.8 to 1.34; 72 participants, one trial; metrifonate 3 x 10 mg/kg at three months: RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.07 to 1.57; 100 participants, one trial). In one trial, both drugs performed poorly, while in another, both performed well. Other Drugs: Three trials evaluated the antimalarial drug artesunate, but the results were inconsistent. Substantial antischistosomal effects were observed in only one of the three trials, which had an unclear risk of bias due to poor reporting of trial methods. Similarly, another antimalarial drug, mefloquine, was evaluated in two small trials, but the results were inconsistent. Adverse events for all evaluated drugs were generally described as mild, but the quality of adverse event monitoring and reporting was low. Conclusions: Praziquantel at a dose of 40 mg/kg is the most extensively studied drug for treating urinary schistosomiasis and has the strongest evidence base. Potential strategies to improve treatment include combining praziquantel with metrifonate or with antimalarial drugs that have antischistosomal properties, such as artesunate and mefloquine. However, rigorous, adequately powered trials with standardized outcome measures are needed to evaluate these combinations.
